📘 Binary Trees – Part 1 (Introduction & Basics)

🔹 1. Introduction

  • Yeh lecture Binary Trees ka introduction hai
  • Pehle tumne yeh data structures dekhe honge:
    • Arrays
    • Stacks
    • Queues
    • Linked List

👉 Yeh sab Linear Data Structures hote hain

🔹 2. Linear vs Hierarchical

✔ Linear Data Structure

  • Data ek line me hota hai
  • Example: Array → ek ke baad ek

✔ Hierarchical Data Structure

  • Data tree structure me hota hai (parent-child relation)
  • Example:
    • Computer folders 📁
      • Ek folder ke andar dusra folder
      • Uske andar aur folders

👉 Isi type ka structure Tree kehlata hai

🔹 3. What is a Binary Tree?

  • "Binary" ka matlab hota hai → 0 ya 1 / ya max 2
  • Binary Tree me:
    • Har node ke maximum 2 children ho sakte hain

👉 Example samajh lo:

  • Ek node ke:
    • 0 child ho sakte hain
    • 1 child ho sakta hai
    • ya max 2 children

❌ 3 children allowed nahi hain

🔹 4. Why Binary Trees Important?

  • Interviews me bahut common topic hai
  • DSA ka major part hai
  • Problems frequently poochi jaati hain

👉 Isliye pura series banaya gaya hai

🔹 5. Basic Terminologies

🔹 Quick Recap

  • Root → starting node
  • Children → niche wale nodes
  • Leaf → jinke children nahi
  • Subtree → node + uske niche sab
  • Ancestors → upar wale sab nodes

Binary Trees – Part 2 (Types of Binary Trees)

🔹 1. Types of Binary Trees

Total 5 types discuss kiye gaye:

  1. Full Binary Tree
  2. Complete Binary Tree
  3. Perfect Binary Tree
  4. Balanced Binary Tree
  5. Degenerate (Skewed) Tree

🔸 2. Full Binary Tree

✔ Definition:

  • Har node ke:
    • ya toh 0 children honge
    • ya exactly 2 children honge

👉 Simple:

  • 1 child allowed nahi hai ❌

✔ Valid Example:

  • Node → 2 children ✔
  • Node → 0 children ✔

❌ Invalid Example:

  • Agar kisi node ka sirf 1 child hai
    👉 Toh wo Full Binary Tree nahi hai

🔹 Shortcut:

👉 “0 ya 2 children only”

🔸 3. Complete Binary Tree

✔ Definition:

  • Sab levels completely filled hone chahiye
  • Except last level
  • Last level me:
    • Nodes left side me hone chahiye

✔ Valid Cases:

Case 1:

  • Har level full ✔

Case 2:

  • Last level incomplete hai
  • But nodes left side me hain ✔


same depth ho mtlb yeh c pe ruk jaata dikkt hojati h and jo jo c ka h woh left me hi ho 

❌ Invalid Case:

  • Last level me gap hai aur node right side me hai

👉 Example:

  • Left empty, right filled ❌

🔹 Shortcut:

👉 “Last level tak left se fill hona chahiye”

🔸 4. Perfect Binary Tree

A binary tree of height 'h' having the maximum number of nodes is a perfect binary tree. 
For a given height h, the maximum number of nodes is 2h+1-1.

✔ Definition:

  • Sab leaf nodes same level pe hone chahiye

✔ Valid:

  • Har leaf same depth pe hai ✔

❌ Invalid:

  • Leaf nodes different levels pe hain ❌

🔹 Shortcut:

👉 “All leaves at same level”

🔸 5. Balanced Binary Tree

✔ Definition:

  • Tree ki height ≈ log(n) honi chahiye
    (n = number of nodes)

✔ Meaning:

  • Tree zyada lamba (skewed) nahi hona chahiye
  • Balanced hona chahiye for efficiency

✔ Example:

  • n = 8
  • log₂(8) ≈ 3
    👉 Height ≈ 3 honi chahiye

❌ Invalid:

  • Agar tree straight line ban gaya
    👉 Height bahut badh jayegi

🔹 Why Important?

  • Fast searching ke liye
  • Time complexity improve hoti hai

🔸 6. Degenerate (Skewed) Tree

✔ Definition:

  • Har node ka sirf 1 child hota hai

✔ Structure:

  • Tree ek linked list jaisa ban jata hai

✔ Types:

  1. Left Skewed
  2. Right Skewed

❌ Problem:

  • Height = n
    👉 Very inefficient

🔹 Shortcut:

👉 “Tree → Linked List jaisa”

🔹 Final Quick Summary

TypeRule
Full0 ya 2 children
CompleteLast level left se fill
PerfectAll leaves same level
BalancedHeight ≈ log(n)

📘 Binary Trees – Representation in C++ (Hinglish Notes)

🔹 1. Basic Idea

  • Binary Tree ko C++ me represent karne ke liye:
    👉 Nodes + Pointers use hote hain
  • Har node ke paas hota hai:
    • Data (value)
    • Left pointer
    • Right pointer

🔸 2. Node Structure Concept

👉 Har node kuch aisa hota hai:

  • Ek value store karta hai
  • Left child ko point karta hai
  • Right child ko point karta hai

✔ Example Tree:

        5
       / \
      6   7
     / \  /
    8   9 10

✔ Pointer Understanding:

  • Node 5:
    • left → 6
    • right → 7
  • Node 6:
    • left → 8
    • right → 9
  • Node 7:
    • left → 10
    • right → NULL
  • Leaf nodes (8, 9, 10):
    • left → NULL
    • right → NULL


🔹 3. Important Rule

👉 Agar kisi node ka child nahi hai:

  • Uska pointer → NULL hota hai

🔸 4. C++ me Node ka Structure

struct Node {
    int data;  // bich wala
    Node* left; // left wala 
    Node* right;  // right wala 

    Node(int val) {
        data = val;
        left = NULL;
        right = NULL;  //  data = val krdenge mtlb koi bhi val and right left ko null kardenge 
    }
};

✔ Explanation:

  • data → value store karega
  • left → left child ka address
  • right → right child ka address

👉 Constructor:

  • Jab node create hota hai:
    • data assign hota hai
    • left & right = NULL

🔹 5. Tree Creation in Main Function

✔ Step-by-step:

Node* root = new Node(1);

👉 Root node create ho gaya (value = 1)

root->left = new Node(2);
root->right = new Node(3);

👉 Ab tree:

    1
   / \
  2   3

✔ Bigger Tree Example:

root->left->left = new Node(4);
root->left->right = new Node(5);

👉 Final tree:

        1
       / \
      2   3
     / \
    4   5

🔹 6. Key Understanding

  • -> ka matlab:
    👉 pointer ke through access
  • new Node(x):
    👉 new node create karta hai

🔹 7. Important Observations

  • Tree manually banaya ja sakta hai
  • Har node dynamically create hota hai
  • Structure flexible hota hai

🔹 8. Quick Summary

  • Binary Tree = Nodes + Pointers
  • Har node:
    • data + left + right
  • Leaf nodes → NULL pointers
  • C++ me:
    • struct Node use hota hai
  • Tree create:
    • new Node() se

📘 Binary Trees – Traversals (DFS & BFS) – Hinglish Notes

🔹 1. Why Traversal Important?

  • Tree me problems solve karne ke liye:
    👉 Tumhe tree traverse (visit) karna padega
  • Without traversal:
    ❌ Tum nodes access hi nahi kar paoge

🔹 2. Types of Traversal

2 main types:

  1. Depth First Search (DFS)
  2. Breadth First Search (BFS)

🌳 DEPTH FIRST SEARCH (DFS)

👉 Depth me jaate hain (deep → subtree → phir back)

🔸 DFS ke 3 Types

  1. Inorder
  2. Preorder
  3. Postorder

🔹 3. Inorder Traversal (Left → Root → Right)

✔ Rule:

👉 Left → Root → Right

✔ Example Tree:

        1
      /   \
     2     3
    / \   / \
   4   5 6   7

✔ Steps:

  • Left subtree → 4 2 5 (lefttest side cover kro )
  • Root → 1 ( root pe aao)
  • Right subtree → 6 3 7 (rightest side pe aao) 

✔ Final Answer:

👉 4 2 5 1 6 3 7

🔹 Trick:

👉 Root beech me aata hai

🔹 4. Preorder Traversal (Root → Left → Right)

✔ Rule:

👉 Root → Left → Right

✔ Steps:

  • Root → 1
  • Left → 2 4 5
  • Right → 3 6 7

✔ Final Answer:

👉 1 2 4 5 3 6 7

🔹 Trick:

👉 Root sabse pehle

🔹 5. Postorder Traversal (Left → Right → Root)

✔ Rule:

👉 Left → Right → Root

✔ Steps:

  • Left → 4 5 2
  • Right → 6 7 3
  • Root → 1

✔ Final Answer:

👉 4 5 2 6 7 3 1

🔹 Trick:

👉 Root sabse last

👉 Har subtree pe same logic repeat hota hai (Recursion)

  • Subtree = mini tree
  • Same rule apply karo

🔹 9. BFS (Level Order Traversal)

✔ Concept:

👉 Tree ko level by level traverse karte hain

✔ Same Example:

Binary Trees – Level Order Traversal (BFS) + Code

🔹 1. What is Level Order Traversal?

👉 Isko Breadth First Search (BFS) bhi kehte hain

✔ Concept:

  • Tree ko level by level traverse karte hain
  • Har level ko left → right order me print karte hain

✔ Example Tree:

        1
      /   \
     2     3
    / \   / \
   4   5 6   7

✔ Level-wise Traversal:

  • Level 0 → 1
  • Level 1 → 2 3
  • Level 2 → 4 5 6 7

✔ Final Output:

👉 1 2 3 4 5 6 7

🔹 2. Key Idea

👉 BFS ke liye hum use karte hain:

  • Queue (FIFO)

🔹 3. Algorithm (Step-by-Step)

✔ Step 1:

  • Queue me root daalo

👉 queue = [1]

✔ Step 2:

  • Queue se element nikalo (pop)
  • Uske:
    • Left child add karo
    • Right child add karo

✔ Step 3:

  • Har level ke nodes ko ek list me store karo

✔ Step 4:

  • Repeat until queue empty


🔹 4. Detailed Flow

🔸 Iteration 1:

  • Queue: [1]
  • Output: [1] 1 ke dono bche daale vector ke andar vector me 
  • Add → 2, 3 then 2 or quie me daaldiye 

👉 Queue: [2, 3]

🔸 Iteration 2:

  • Queue: [2, 3]
  • Output: [2, 3] for 2 and 3 unke left and right daalenge in the vector 
  • jb yeh dal rhe honge vector me toh yeh pop hojayenge 
  • Add → 4, 5, 6, 7  fir inke saare bche list me daaleng e

👉 Queue: [4, 5, 6, 7]

🔸 Iteration 3:

  • Queue: [4, 5, 6, 7]
  • Out  put: [4, 5, 6, 7]  now inke left right dalenge 
  • No children

👉 Queue empty ✅

🔹 5. Data Structures Used

  • Queue → traversal ke liye
  • Vector of Vector → level-wise answer store karne ke liye

🔹 6. C++ Code

vector<vector<int>> levelOrder(Node* root) {
    vector<vector<int>> ans;

    if (root == NULL) return ans;

    queue<Node*> q; // ek queue bnayi 
    q.push(root);   // fir us queue me root push kari

    while (!q.empty()) { // jb tk q empty nhi hoajti yeh chelga 
        int size = q.size();  // its q me jitne element h utha ek size me store krlenge
        vector<int> level;    // ek vector bnate h 

        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) { // loop chalyenge jo push krega vector me 
                                        // fir woh vector baadme main vector me push hoga 
            Node* node = q.front();     // jo chij top pe h pdki 
            q.pop();                   // top wali chij ko nikal diya 

            level.push_back(node->data); // apne level naam ke array me push kiya 

            if (node->left) q.push(node->left);  // us node ke dono left right push kiye 
            if (node->right) q.push(node->right);
        }

        ans.push_back(level);  // then at last usko hi push kardiya 
    }

    return ans;
}

🔹 7. Important Concept

👉 size = q.size() kyu use kiya?

  • Yeh batata hai:
    👉 current level me kitne nodes hain

👉 Taaki hum level-by-level process kar saken

I. Introduction and Definition of a Path
  • Definition: A path is defined as starting from any node and going to any node.
  • Rule: In a path, a single node will only occur once.
  • The Problem: In a binary tree, there can be multiple paths. You need to figure out which path gives the maximum summation.
  • Objective: Write a program that returns this maximum path sum.
II. Naive Solution and Complexity
  • Logic: A naive approach might involve trying out every possible pair of nodes in the tree.
  • Complexity: This is complicated and would take O(N2) combinations.
  • Prerequisites: To understand the optimized approach, it is highly recommended to check out videos on finding the maximum height and the diameter of a binary tree.
III. The Optimized Logic
  • Standing at a Node: For any given node, you figure out the maximum left sum and the maximum right sum.
  • The Formula: For a node to find its maximum path sum, the formula is: Node Value + Left Sum + Right Sum.

  • Global Maximum: You maintain a global variable (e.g., maxi) to keep track of the maximum path sum found across all nodes during the traversal.


  • Handling Negative Sums:
    • If a path from the left or right subtree returns a negative value, it will only decrease your total sum.
    • Therefore, you should ignore all negative path sums coming from the left or right.
    • In the code, this is handled by taking max(0, recursive_call).

      int right = max(0, maxPathDown(node->right, maxi));


IV. Step-by-Step Example Walkthrough (Dry Run) The subtitles use a specific tree example: Root (-10) with Left (9) and Right (20). Node 20 has children 15 (left) and 7 (right).
  1. Node 9:
    • It calls its left and right, which return 0.
    • Its path sum is 9+0+0=9. Update maxi to 9.
    • It returns its own value (9) to its parent.
  2. Node 15:
    • Calls left/right (0). Path sum = 15+0+0=15. Update maxi to 15.
    • Returns 15 to its parent.
  3. Node 7:
    • Calls left/right (0). Path sum = 7+0+0=7. maxi remains 15.

  5. Root Node (-10):
    • It receives 9 from the left and 35 from the right.
    • Its path sum is −10+9+35=34.
    • Since 34 is not greater than the current maxi (42), the global maximum remains 42.

Detailed Notes: Algorithmic Verification of Identical Binary Trees

I. Introduction and Problem Definition

  • This lecture covers the problem of checking if two binary trees are identical, which is part of the "tree series".
  • The Problem: You are given two binary trees, T1 and T2.
  • The Goal: Determine if tree T1 is identical to tree T2.
  • Output:
    • If the trees are identical, return True.
    • If they are not identical, return False.
  • Example 1 (Identical): If T1 is identical in structure and value to T2, the answer is true.
  • Example 2 (Not Identical): If even one node value is different, or if a node is missing (e.g., one tree has a node and the other has null at that position), they are not identical.

II. Selecting a Traversal Approach

  • To solve this problem, you can use any traversal you prefer: Preorder, Inorder, or Postorder.
  • The logic remains that you must traverse both trees simultaneously and compare them at every step.

  • The idea is to perform a traversal on both trees at the same time.
  • Dry Run Flow:

    2. If the root values are the same (e.g., both are 1), move to the left in both trees.
    3. Compare the left nodes. If they match (e.g., both are 2), continue moving left.
    4. If you reach a null on the left side of both trees, it means that part is identical.
    5. Once the left side is finished, come back and move to the right side of the current node and repeat the comparison.
  • If at any instance the nodes do not match, the trees are not identical.

  1. Check if both are null: If node1 is null and node2 is null, they are identical at this point. Return true.

    • If the values are not the same (node1.val != node2.val), return false.

    • return (node1.val == node2.val) && isSame(node1.left, node2.left) && isSame(node1.right, node2.right).

    • Example Binary Tree Traversal:
      • From the right side, at the first level, you see Node 1.
      • At the second level, you see Node 3 (Node 2 is covered by 3).
      • At the third level, you see Node 7 (Nodes 4 and 5 are hidden by 7).
      • At the bottom, you see Node 6.
    • Final Right View Sequence: 1, 3, 7, 6.
    • The goal is to write a program that prints this view for any given binary tree.

    III. Logical Intuition
    • The Level Rule: The right side view is essentially the last node of every level.
      • 1 is the last node of level 1; 3 is the last of level 2; 7 is the last of level 3; 6 is the last of level 4.
    • Alternative Perspective: If you have a traversal technique that moves from right to left, the first node encountered at every level will be the right view.
    IV. Choosing the Traversal: Recursive vs. Iterative
    • There are two main ways to solve this: Recursive (Inorder, Preorder, Postorder) or Iterative (Level Order).
    • Iterative (Level Order) Analysis:
      • Time Complexity: Big O(N).
      • Space Complexity: At the worst case (full binary tree), the queue might store roughly half the nodes of the tree, which is significant.
    • Recursive Analysis:
      • Time Complexity: Big O(N).
      • Space Complexity: Big O(Height) of the tree. In a skew tree, this could become Big O(N).
    • The Decision: The lesson teaches the recursive solution because the code is short and crisp. Interviewers prefer clean, short code over the lenier iterative versions.
    V. The Recursive Algorithm (Reverse Preorder Traversal)
    • The preferred traversal is the reverse preorder traversal.
    • Standard Preorder: Root, Left, Right.
    • Reverse Preorder: Root, Right, Left.
    • By moving right to left, the first node reached at every level will be part of the Right View.
    • Function Parameters: The recursive function takes the node and the current level (initially level 0).
    VI. The "Smart Technique" for Storing the View
    • To store the nodes, use a data structure (DS) that starts empty.
    • The Rule: Every time you enter a level for the first time, add that node to the data structure.
    • Logic: If the current level is equal to the size of the data structure (level == ds.size()), it means this is the first time you are visiting this specific level.
    VII. Detailed Step-by-Step Dry Run Using the example tree provided in the subtitles:
    1. Initial Call: Node 1, Level 0. DS is empty (size 0). Since 0 == 0, insert 1.
    2. Move Right: Node 3, Level 1. DS size is 1. Since 1 == 1, insert 3.
    3. Move Right: Node 7, Level 2. DS size is 2. Since 2 == 2, insert 7.
    4. Move Right (from 7): Hits null, return.
    5. Move Left (from 7): Hits null, return.
    6. Backtrack to 3 and move Left: Hits null, return.
    7. Backtrack to 1 and move Left: Node 2, Level 1.
      • The DS size is already 3 (from levels 0, 1, 2).
      • Since 1 != 3, Node 2 is not added.
    8. Continuing through Level 2: Move right to Node 5 (Level 2). 2 != 3, so not added.
    9. Reaching the Bottom: Eventually, the traversal reaches Node 6 at Level 3.
      • Since the current level (3) is equal to the DS size (3), insert 6.
    10. This ensures only the first node encountered at each level from the right side is stored.

    • To find the left side view, the logic is identical but the traversal order is swapped.

    IV. The Algorithm Logic (Recursion and Backtracking)
    • Initially, start at the root with an empty data structure (array or vector).
    • Step 1: If the current node is not null, take the node and insert it into your array.
    • Step 2: Check if the current node is equivalent to the target node you are looking for.

    • Step 5 (Backtracking): If both the left and right calls return false (meaning the node is not on either path), you must remove the current guy from the array (pop back) and return false.
    • Step 6: If either the left or right call gives you a true, it means you have found the path. Don't remove the node and just pass on true all the way back up to the root.

    • The problem involves a binary tree where you must ensure it follows the children sum property.
    • The Property: For any node, its value should be equivalent to the left node's value plus the right node's value.

    III. Rules for Modification
    • If a node does not follow the children sum property, you can only increment the values of the nodes.
    • You can increment a node's value by any number of times (+1,+10,+100, etc.).
    • Crucial Constraint: You cannot decrease the value of any node because you could end up with a value of zero or a situation where you can't fulfill the property later.
    • You are allowed to change the entire structure of the tree values to meet the property.
    IV. The Challenge and Inefficiency of Naive Solutions
    • The problem is not as simple as it looks at first sight.
    • If you simply update a node to match its children, you might find that the parent node no longer follows the property because its child's value just changed.
    • There is no guarantee that increasing a value at one level won't break the property at another.
    • Most articles propose a Big O(N²) solution, but this video teaches a linear Big O(N) solution that works in a single traversal.
    V. The Optimized Algorithm Logic
    • The algorithm uses a recursive traversal (move left, move right, then come back).
    • Phase 1: Moving Down (Increasing Values)
      • As you go down the tree, check the sum of the children.
      • Case 1: Children Sum >= Node Value. If the sum of the left and right children is greater than or equal to the current node, update the node's value to be equal to that sum.
      • Case 2: Children Sum < Node Value. If the children's sum is less than the parent node, reassign both the left and right children's values to be equal to the parent node's value.
      • Why this works: By "throwing down" the larger value to the children, you ensure that you are never short of numbers when you eventually backtrack.
    • Phase 2: Backtracking (Summing Up)
      • Once you reach the leaf nodes and start coming back up, the logic changes.
      • For every node you visit while backtracking, take the sum of its (now updated) left and right children.
      • Assign this sum back to the current node.
      • Since you increased the values while going down, the sum of the children will always be greater than or equal to the original node value when you return.

    /**
 * Definition for a binary tree node.
 * struct TreeNode {
 *     int val;
 *     TreeNode *left;
 *     TreeNode *right;
 *     TreeNode() : val(0), left(nullptr), right(nullptr) {}
 *     TreeNode(int x) : val(x), left(nullptr), right(nullptr) {}
 *     TreeNode(int x, TreeNode *left, TreeNode *right)
 *         : val(x), left(left), right(right) {}
 * };
 */

class Solution {
public:

    // -----------------------------
    // STEP 1:
    // Har node ka parent store karna.
    // Example:
    //      3
    //     / \
    //    5   1
    //
    // parent[5] = 3
    // parent[1] = 3
    // -----------------------------
    void markParents(TreeNode* root,
                     unordered_map<TreeNode*, TreeNode*>& parent_track)
    {
        queue<TreeNode*> q;

        q.push(root);

        while(!q.empty())
        {
            TreeNode* current = q.front();
            q.pop();

            // Left child exist karta hai
            if(current->left)
            {
                parent_track[current->left] = current;

                q.push(current->left);
            }

            // Right child exist karta hai
            if(current->right)
            {
                parent_track[current->right] = current;

                q.push(current->right);
            }
        }
    }

    vector<int> distanceK(TreeNode* root, TreeNode* target, int k)
    {
        // Parent mapping banayi
        unordered_map<TreeNode*, TreeNode*> parent_track;
        markParents(root, parent_track);

        // Visited map
        // Infinite loop rokne ke liye
        unordered_map<TreeNode*, bool> visited;

        // BFS Queue
        queue<TreeNode*> q;

        // BFS target node se start hogi
        q.push(target);
        visited[target] = true;

        int curr_level = 0;

        // BFS
        while(!q.empty())
        {
            // Agar K distance tak aa gaye
            if(curr_level == k)
                break;

            curr_level++;

            int size = q.size();

            // Current level ke saare nodes process karo
            for(int i=0;i<size;i++)
            {
                TreeNode* current = q.front();
                q.pop();

                // ---------------------
                // LEFT CHILD
                // ---------------------
                if(current->left &&
                   !visited[current->left])
                {
                    q.push(current->left);

                    visited[current->left] = true;
                }

                // ---------------------
                // RIGHT CHILD
                // ---------------------
                if(current->right &&
                   !visited[current->right])
                {
                    q.push(current->right);

                    visited[current->right] = true;
                }

                // ---------------------
                // PARENT
                // ---------------------
                if(parent_track[current] &&
                   !visited[parent_track[current]])
                {
                    q.push(parent_track[current]);

                    visited[parent_track[current]] = true;
                }
            }
        }

        // Queue me ab sirf distance K wale nodes bache hain

        vector<int> ans;

        while(!q.empty())
        {
            ans.push_back(q.front()->val);

            q.pop();
        }

        return ans;
    }
};

    III. Method 1: Recursive Solution (Reverse Post-Order)

    • Logical Intuition: To flatten the tree without losing track of nodes, the algorithm uses a "reverse post-order" traversal: Right → Left → Root.

    • The Global Pointer: You maintain a variable, previous, which is initially set to null.
    • Step-by-Step Logic:
      1. Recursively call the function for the right subtree.
      2. Recursively call the function for the left subtree.

      • This continues, effectively stacking nodes in reverse order so that when you reach the root (1), its right is already pointing to the correctly flattened subtrees.
    • Complexity:
      • Time Complexity: Big O(N).
      • Space Complexity: Big O(N) (in the worst case of a skewed tree) due to the auxiliary recursive stack space.
    IV. Method 2: Iterative Solution (Using a Stack)
    • The Logic: This method uses an explicit stack to mimic the pre-order traversal while modifying pointers.
    • Step-by-Step Algorithm:
      1. Push the root onto the stack.
      2. While the stack is not empty:
        • Pop the current node (curr).
        • If curr has a right child, push it onto the stack.
        • If curr has a left child, push it onto the stack.
        • If the stack is not empty, point curr.right to the top of the stack.
        • Set curr.left = null.
    • Why Right then Left? Because the stack is Last-In-First-Out (LIFO), pushing the right child first ensures the left child is processed first, maintaining the correct pre-order (Root, Left, Right) flow.

    V. Method 3: Optimized O(1) Space Solution (Morris Traversal Logic)


    • Intuition: For any node, the entire right subtree must be attached to the rightmost node of the left subtree.
    • Step-by-Step Algorithm:
      1. Start with a pointer curr at the root.
      2. While curr is not null:
        • If curr has a left child:
          • Find the rightmost node in the left subtree (let's call it prev).
          • Connect prev.right = curr.right.
          • Connect curr.right = curr.left.
          • Set curr.left = null.
        • Move curr to its right (curr = curr.right).
    • Result: This "threads" the tree into a single right-leaning path without using any extra stack space.
    • Complexity:
      • Time Complexity: Big O(N).
      • Space Complexity: Big O(1) (constant space).
